chapter_theme: At the Vidyadhara princess's vina contest Gandharvadattai, seeing Civakan, loses her self-containment and vows to garland him; Civakan rejects her vinas one by one for faults in their wood and strings, plays and sings rain-season songs that overcome gods, beasts and kings, and the princess, judging the music his, begins her answering song of a woman's pallor in separation.

cast.role: the hero, who comes to the Vidyadhara princess's vina contest
daughter of the Vidyadhara king, defeated by Civakan at the vina
Gandharvadattai's companions and maids, one of whom passes the vina
one of Civakan's party, who hands him strings
kings who came seeking the princess
the people of the earth, who listen
the kinnaras, celestial musicians, who listen

709.reading: With such words the princess's maids rejoice too, and those who look on the bee-tressed one, the limit of all beauty and a goddess to be worshipped with joined hands, each become fixed on whatever part of her their eyes reach.
709.nuance: Who speaks the 'such words' and whom 'those who saw' see is not settled by the verse: the preceding verses give the women's talk about Civakan, and கடவுள் here can be read as the princess herself or as the man she worships; the last line's repeated எனைய/அனைய makes each viewer become what part they reached.

710.reading: The girl whose eyes outdo all the pool's lilies stands as desire, rising like a sea, breaks the fence of shame set round the prison of her self-containment and sets her alight, so that she stands like wax in fire.
710.nuance: The architecture is double: நிறை is the prison (சிறை) and நாண் the fence (வேலி) around it; desire does not break nirai directly but pushes over the fence that guards it.
710.event: Gandharvadattai, seeing Civakan, is overcome by desire.

711.reading: She wonders whether the chest of the youth who churns her, with her beauty as the churning stick, his strength and youth as the rope and his noble birth as the hand that pulls it, till sweet desire foams up, will ever be joined to her.
711.nuance: The image is the churning of the sea for nectar turned inward: her own beauty is the stick, and his qualities are the rope and hands that work it.
711.event: Gandharvadattai longs to be joined to Civakan.

712.reading: She tells her heart not to lament before the flower-haired women for the man whose beauty she drank with her eyes like untouched honey hanging on a sweet cane, and she seems like the bliss won by those who have conquered swelling desire.
712.nuance: The last line compares the love-struck princess to the joy of those who have overcome desire, a striking figure in a Jain epic: the supreme measure of delight is the ascetic's, applied here to the very desire it conquers.
712.event: Gandharvadattai bids her heart hide its longing from the women about her.

713.reading: She asks who among men he can be, the man of great beauty caught in the net of her eyes, held in her grasp, who has brought her to this state, bearing a spear like red fire taken form.
713.nuance: The second line, பெண்ணெனும் உழலை பாயும், is hard: it may say that he leaps the barrier that womanhood sets, or that he is the one at whom the bar of women strains; the reading turns on it.

714.reading: Whoever he is, she says, he has opened the door of her hard self-containment, entered the virgin chamber of her guarded heart and bound it till it aches, and she in turn will bind him fast with a garland as the gods are bound, if he will only wait a little.
714.nuance: The vow answers binding with binding: he tied her heart, she will tie him with the marriage garland, which she does in 738.
714.event: Gandharvadattai resolves to garland the unknown youth.

715.reading: Fainting like a doe whose mate has taken a thrown spear in the wasteland, she opens her eyes, sighs hotly, trembles, and clinging to her companion as a creeper clings to a creeper so that the bees fly from the companion's hair, asks her to carry this sweet lute to the man of the handsome chest.
715.event: Gandharvadattai swoons and asks her companion to take a lute to Civakan.

716.reading: At the wide-eyed princess's bidding the long-eyed maid draws back the curtain and holds out a vina, and the lion-strong youth, saying 'let it come', takes it and looks it over, meaning to declare the full reach of his knowledge.
716.event: A maid passes a vina through the curtain and Civakan takes it to judge it.

717.reading: The man of wide learning, as abundant as the rain the swollen sky bears in labour, touches the strings of the golden lute so they hum like bees, and, looking at the woman who stands by, tells her in music what is wrong with the lady's vina.
717.nuance: His judgement is given 'in music' (இசையின்), so the examination of the instrument is already a performance.
717.event: Civakan tries the first vina and begins to name its faults.

718.reading: He rejects vina after vina: this one was softened by standing in water, this one drifted in on a flood, this one bears a sword wound, this one was struck by thunder, and this one has no worth, like the son of a famed courtesan.
718.nuance: Each fault is a fault of the tree the wood came from, so the instruments are judged by their origin; the last is put in human terms, birth from a courtesan, and spoken by a hero whose own birth is at this point hidden and who passes as a merchant's son.
718.event: Civakan rejects several vinas, naming the defect of each one's wood.

claims.claim: a courtesan's son lacks the standing of good birth

719.reading: Telling the girl of the bright breasts that this one, like those burned by the fire of desire, was scorched and warped when farmers burned the clearing, and this one cracked when an elephant rubbed against its tree, he sends them back, and when a good lute in a smoke-scented cloth cover is held out he takes it and says it is sound.
719.nuance: The simile 'like those burned by the fire of desire' brings the princess's state (710) into the inspection of a burnt instrument.
719.event: Civakan rejects two more vinas and accepts a lute brought in its cover.

720.reading: He tells the lute's descent: its tree was born of the great earth-maiden and nursed by the sky as foster mother, who fed it the sweet milk of rain from cloud breasts with lightning for a golden cord, so that, free of the four diseases, it grew to rare beauty and was cut by the blade's edge.
720.nuance: The good wood is given a pedigree like a person's, a mother who bore it and a foster mother (கைத்தாய்) who reared it; 'the four diseases' are presumably the defects just listed, though the verse does not name them.
720.event: Civakan declares the origin of the accepted lute's wood.

721.reading: In no time he tells the faults of the strings, untwists one to show the princess the hair caught in it, and as people say the fragrant-haired one has lost to the rich youth, he takes fresh long-twisted strings from Nabulan's hand.
721.nuance: The first defeat is in judgement, before any playing: the princess's instrument is shown to be flawed down to a hair in a string.
721.event: Civakan exposes a hair in the strings and takes new strings from Nabulan, and the onlookers say the princess has lost.

722.reading: Taking the fine lute with its golden bowl hard to fashion, coral pegs of many works, gem-polished ivory stem, diamond tuning knob and strings like nectar flowing as honey, the youth whom the astrologers praised sets out to hold the sea-girt world in its sound.
722.nuance: The parts named (பத்தர், ஆணி, மருப்பு, மாடகம், நரம்பு) are the classical lute's anatomy; கணிபுகழ் காளை recalls the horoscope of 539.
722.event: Civakan takes up the restrung lute to play.

723.reading: Tuning the kural string as the ground note, the youth with the garland hanging in his locks draws music with his fingers that none can tell from a voice; gods and men fall, birds and beasts droop, trees and stones melt, and having listened he rises into song.
723.nuance: குரல் is both the first note of the scale and the voice, and the line plays on both; whether the falling and melting follow the playing or the singing that begins in line 4 is not clear.
723.event: Civakan tunes and plays, and all beings are overcome, before he begins to sing.

724.reading: The first song asks whether to call it the cloud that flashes and thunders till the young snake is shaken, or the breast pressed by the golden cord of the girl who wastes away at the lightning-lit rain.
724.nuance: Each stanza of the song sets a rain-season scene against a woman's distress at it; that the rain grieves her implies an absent man, but the song never says so.

725.reading: The second asks whether to call it the hill where waterfalls cry under the rain the cloud pours, or the heart of the soft-graced woman who grieves to see that hill of crying falls.

726.reading: The third asks whether to call it the rain season that set the forest budding and flowering like the stars of the sky, or the honey-garlanded woman who grieves at the sight of that flowering season.

727.reading: Seeing how the lord's jewelled fingers crept over the strings and the beauty of his singing that kept the rhythm, the gods let fall their vinas, the Vidyadharas melted and drooped, the people of the earth swooned in wonder and the siddhas kept it in their hearts.
727.event: Gods, Vidyadharas, men and siddhas are overcome by Civakan's playing.

728.reading: Seeing how the bees falling dazed tore the garlands, and how the vina's strings and the man's jewel-like throat worked as one, the kinnaras with their garlands drooped.
728.nuance: ஊழ் in ஊழ்மணி மிடறு here seems to mean order or ripeness of the voice, not fate; the verse makes no claim about karma.
728.event: The kinnaras are overcome by the unison of voice and strings.

729.reading: He sang so that the gods marvelled, the Vidyadhara heroes praised him with longing, men rejoiced, the birds of the sky forgot their bodies and dropped, and Kama himself was put to shame, while all the kings became like dolls painted in a picture.
729.event: Civakan's song leaves the assembled kings motionless.

730.reading: Thinking that song and lute have both gone over to Civakan as a kite's shadow goes with the kite, the spear-eyed girl like a young peahen sits to tune her lute as his guest's due and to lose at the vina.
730.nuance: தோற்பான் can be read as purpose, 'in order to lose', which would make her defeat a choice, or as describing her as the one who is to lose; the verse leaves it open.
730.event: Gandharvadattai, judging herself outmatched, sits to play her turn.

731.reading: Her garland hanging down her back, her earrings and gold ear-ornaments gleaming, her lovely brow sweating, the peerless girl turns her neck aside and begins to sing a sweet song.

732.reading: Her song asks a friend of sweet, skilled speech whether, when the breasts that bear jewels of flame and the bow-curved brow are drowned in red pallor, while the mountain's falls flash like a sword, the lovers do not see.
732.nuance: This is the first of three stanzas (733 and 734 repeat it with variations); the song is a woman's complaint in separation, sung by a princess who has never been separated, and its refrain காணார்கொல் கேள்வர் makes the pallor a sign meant for the absent man.

links.note: Gandharvadattai's vow to bind the unknown youth with a garland is kept when she fastens the gold garland on his chest after the contest.
links.teaches: The garland in 738 is the answer to an inward vow, so the public result of the contest was settled in her heart before a string was touched.

links.note: The astrologer's reading places the princess's destined husband in Rajamapuram; as Civakan takes the lute the poet calls him கணிபுகழ் காளை, the youth the astrologers praised.
links.teaches: The epithet at the moment of playing marks the contest as the working out of the horoscope, so the reader hears the song as a prophecy being fulfilled rather than a match in doubt.

links.note: The lute's wood is born of the earth-maiden and reared by the sky as foster mother; Civakan, born in the burning ground, was handed by Kantukkatan to a foster mother.
links.teaches: The instrument Civakan chooses has his own hidden history, a mother who bore it and another who reared it, while the ones he rejects are faulted for their origin, so his judgement of pedigree reflects on the birth no one at the contest knows.

links.note: In both a woman takes the lute after the man's songs and begins her own; the Cintamani's நிலத்தோர் and gods wondering (729) echo the Silappathikaram's நிலத்தெய்வம் வியப்பு எய்த, and both close on பாடத் தொடங்கு-.
links.teaches: The same turn at the lute, his songs then hers, ends in a garland in the Cintamani and in Kovalan's leaving in the Silappathikaram, which shows that the outcome lies in how the man hears her reply, as yielding or as a hidden intent.

links.note: The Kural's woman says desire's axe breaks the door of nirai bolted with shame; the princess says the youth has opened the door of her hard nirai and entered her heart's guarded chamber.
links.teaches: The Cintamani keeps the Kural's door of nirai but changes the breaker from desire to the man and the outcome from lament to a vow of marriage, so the breach of self-containment can be the start of a lawful bond.

gains.a: the princess's image is read with the Kural's exact logic of door and bolt, so her 'hard nirai' is a guarded virtue, not a figure of speech
gains.b: the couplet's breach, spoken by a woman already in love, gains a first-sight case in an unmarried girl, where it leads to the garland instead of grief

links.note: The Kural's lover says the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness; the epic's princess has a sea of desire that overruns the fence of shame round her nirai.
links.teaches: Shame is a raft for the Kural's man and a fence round a prison for the epic's woman, so the same flood threatens a man's means of crossing but a woman's enclosure.

gains.a: the princess's sea of desire is placed in the Kural's account of what desire sweeps away, naming shame as the first loss
gains.b: the couplet, spoken by a man, gains the woman's version, where shame guards nirai rather than carrying her

links.note: Both describe the lute part by part with the same names, the bowl (பத்தர், பத்தல்), the pegs (ஆணி), the stem (மருப்பு) and the strings (நரம்பு), and both credit its music with power over the hostile and the wild.
links.teaches: The Cintamani takes over the Sangam bard's catalogue of the lute but makes it gold, coral and diamond, and makes knowing the instrument's parts and faults the contest itself, so the bard's working tool becomes the test of a prince.

gains.a: the epic's list of parts is shown to be an inherited form of praise, which explains why the lute is described before it is played
gains.b: the bard's poor lute, praised to win a patron's gift, gains a later setting where judging its wood and strings decides a royal marriage

new_concepts.gloss: music: song and the playing of instruments, as art, skill and power over hearers
